analysis.one_liner: Expands public reporting of toxic chemical releases and requires warnings on children's products containing hazardous chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was introduced in September 1996 and died in a House committee when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required chemical manufacturers and facility operators to report far more about their toxic chemical use, including worker exposures and detailed materials accounting, and would have lowered reporting thresholds for the most dangerous substances like dioxins, lead, mercury, and cadmium. It would also have required warning labels on foods and consumer products aimed at children that contain chemicals identified as carcinogens, reproductive toxins, or neurotoxins, and would have mandated federal screening for endocrine-disrupting chemicals. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents, consumers, workers, and communities near industrial facilities. The bill declared a federal policy that the public has a right to know how toxic chemicals are used, and its findings state that without this information parents cannot protect their children, consumers cannot make informed choices, and workers and communities cannot protect themselves [S3]. Workers would gain directly: facilities would have to report how many employees and contractors were exposed to each toxic chemical and estimate occupational exposures [S2][S3]. Communities would gain from lower reporting thresholds for highly toxic, persistent chemicals like dioxin, lead, mercury, cadmium, and chromium, and from coverage of additional facility types [S2][S3]. Citizens would gain new enforcement rights, including private lawsuits with attorney fees against violators [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents, workers, and communities near polluting facilities

how_it_helps.text: Requires facilities to report the number of employees and contractors exposed to each toxic chemical, estimates of occupational exposures, pollution-prevention quantities, and full materials accounting of chemical use, making industry's toxic operations visible to the public [S2][S3].

Directs EPA to set lower reporting thresholds within two years for highly toxic substances, specifically including dioxin, cadmium, chromium, lead, and mercury, so that releases well below the current 10,000-pound threshold must be disclosed [S2][S3].

Bars businesses from knowingly exposing children under 7 to federally listed carcinogens, reproductive toxins, or neurotoxins in children's foods or products without a clear warning label at the point of sale [S2][S3].

Requires EPA screening of any substance to which a substantial population may be exposed for endocrine-disrupting effects, and lets such a finding trigger regulation of the substance as hazardous under toxic substances law [S2][S3].
Gives citizens and workers the right to sue violators and to win attorney fees, and tightens trade-secret rules so companies cannot easily hide chemical information from the public [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers, processors, and users, who would bear the cost of generating exposure data, detailed materials accounting, additional testing, and warning labels for children's products containing listed chemicals [S2][S3]. The reporting burden would fall on a broadened set of covered facilities, including additional industry categories identified by EPA [S2][S3]. The bill's own findings concede disclosure imposes a burden on business, but argue it is lesser than mandatory controls [S3].

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden would be real: the bill adds worker-exposure reporting, annual materials accounting, expanded facility coverage, and child-product warning labels, and businesses with fewer than 50 employees and public entities are exempted in recognition that smaller operations would find it harder to comply [S2][S3].

Warning labels on foods and products could impose costs that flow to consumers in prices, and the children's disclosure scheme relies on EPA compiling lists from other agencies' chemical identifications within a year, an administrative task that could be slow or contested [S3].

The enforcement scheme allows private citizen lawsuits with civil penalties up to $25,000 per day or a share of retail sales, which critics of such provisions generally argue invites litigation costs; the bill places the burden of proving a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' exemption on the defendant [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core is disclosure rather than prohibition, the least intrusive form of regulation: companies keep selling their products but must tell the public what toxic chemicals they release and put in children's products, and can avoid labeling by proving no harm. The costs fall on chemical-intensive industries, and some would likely pass through to consumers as prices. The main uncertainty is administrative: the bill leans heavily on EPA to compile chemical lists and set thresholds on tight deadlines. On balance, the public benefits (information that helps parents, workers, and communities avoid exposure) appear to exceed the compliance costs, but the bill never got far enough for that to be tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 1996, referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, and never received a hearing vote or floor action before the 104th Congress ended in early January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey introduced the bill on September 27, 1996, with three Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the same day [S5].
Two weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, chemical manufacturers and other regulated facilities avoided the added reporting, testing, and labeling costs it would have imposed, and the public did not get the expanded disclosures.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical and product manufacturers avoided new disclosure rules

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to the House Commerce Committee.

for.name: Reps. Robert Andrews, Robert Torricelli, and Ed Markey

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood beyond the sponsorship itself [S3][S4].

industries.note: They would have had to generate and disclose worker-exposure data, full materials accounting, and lower-threshold reporting on the most dangerous substances, and tighter trade-secret rules would have limited their ability to withhold information. The bill died, so none of these costs took effect.

industries.industry: Consumer product and food makers (children's products)
industries.note: Sellers of children's foods and products containing listed carcinogens, reproductive toxins, or neurotoxins would have faced warning-label requirements and civil penalties, with a small-business exemption under 50 employees. The bill never advanced.
Coverage would have expanded to additional facility categories and reporting would have covered releases as well as use, adding compliance paperwork. The bill died in committee.
